bands.why: A person who holds at 20 wins most first levels (0.84 measured), never all of them.
The hardest row is close to a coin flip for a reasonable player (0.46 measured).
Holding at random wins fewer than half of the easiest levels (0.41 measured): when to stop matters.
A level lasts a couple of dozen rolls (median 26), about a minute of play.
An endless run outlasts a level (median 70 rolls measured) and still ends.
A reasonable endless run banks more than any level target (median 132 measured).
Busts keep biting in the endless run (7.01 per run measured), so pushing your luck stays a choice.

notes: Pig, four tuning rows on the 0..100 scale sampled at their lower bounds (0/25/50/75), the endless run at 100, 100 seeds. The first run (busts in a row that end the run: 3; turns per row 10/12/14/16) had random play beating the hold-at-20 player on the easiest row (0.72 vs 0.61): 39 of its 100 runs ended in a bust streak, so the rules punished pushing your luck. maxBusts 3 -> 5 restored the skill gap (random 0.54, holdAt20 0.83 at d25) but random still won 0.76 of the easiest levels and the curve fell by only 0.05-0.09 per row. Fewer turns per row (7/9/10/11) gave holdAt20 0.84/0.74/0.63/0.46, random 0.41/0.16/0.04/0 and the lookahead upper bound 0.90 at d25 (8/9/10/11 was rejected: random won 0.56 of the easiest levels). The payoff (a roll that survives, the push-your-luck yes) and the twist (a bust that throws points away) were decided before the first sim run; banks are what the score (medianScore) measures, and the later observation that a bank would have come within 10 rolls in only 65 % of runs is why they are not a tag. The curve step (0.08) and the skill-gap step (0.1) sit below the measured 0.10-0.17 and 0.16. Proposed until a person has played it on an iPhone and an Android phone.
